solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Red alert heard when landing gear's faulty

indicators.note: gear that is faulty is out of order, so these letters are put into a different order

explanation.surface: An alarm sounds in the cockpit because the plane's undercarriage has failed on the approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faulty' asks for the letters of LANDING GEARS (the possessive 's counts as an S here) to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A red alert is a warning of imminent peril, exactly what a warning signal of this kind gives.

clue.text: Comes round in the morning, normally

definitions.text: Comes round in the morning, normally

parts.words: Comes round in the morning, normally
parts.note: to come round is to regain consciousness, and most of us do so on waking at dawn after a night's sleep

explanation.surface: Someone describes their routine of waking up each day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes round' could suggest a visitor calling; here it means waking.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming round from sleep is rousing, and that usually happens at the start of the day.

clue.text: Flower in appropriate place, excellent for mounting

parts.note: a garden is the fitting place for a flower to grow

indicators.note: in a down entry, mounting means going upwards, so the piece is read from the bottom up

parts.note: A1 means first-rate; its digit 1 is read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A bloom is set in a suitable spot, ideal for displaying on a stand.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is the standard crossword way to write 'excellent', with the digit read as I; 'for mounting' reads it upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The gardenia is a fragrant white-flowered shrub, a specific example of a flower.

clue.text: Child's play leads to row over missing props

indicators.note: the leads of words are their front letters, taken here from the four words after

explanation.surface: A school play descends into a squabble because the stage props have gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child's play' looks like a school production but defines a romp.
explanation.definitionFit: A romp is a playful frolic, the boisterous play typical of children.

clue.text: Iron, acid and double nitrogen found in maize

indicators.note: to found metal is to melt and cast it into a new shape, so the letters are remoulded
double means the nitrogen symbol appears twice

parts.note: N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A chemistry analysis lists the elements and compounds detected in a sample of cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found' looks like 'discovered' but is the anagram signal: IRON, ACID and NN are recast.
explanation.definitionFit: Indian corn is the old name for the cereal crop also known as corn in America.

clue.text: Material only manufactured with needles, originally

indicators.note: manufactured goods are made up from raw parts, so these letters are made up anew
originally points to the first letter, the origin, of the word beside it

explanation.surface: A fabric is said to be produced only with knitting needles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manufactured' rearranges ONLY to NYLO, then 'originally' gives N.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fibre and fabric, so it is a material.

clue.text: Nightingale's nightly fuel requirement, presumably

parts.note: Florence Nightingale, the Lady with the Lamp, did night rounds in the Crimea, so her lamp would need filling each evening

explanation.surface: A songbird singing at night apparently needs refuelling.
explanation.walkthrough: Nightingale is not the bird but Florence Nightingale, the Victorian nurse famed as the Lady with the Lamp for her night rounds of wounded soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraffin burned in lanterns is the fuel such a lamp-carrier would need.

clue.text: What prisoners require starting sentence

parts.note: a sentence of written text starts with an upper-case letter; a prisoner condemned to death has a capital sentence

explanation.surface: A description of what convicts need as they begin their prison terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sentence' is grammatical, not judicial: every written sentence opens with an upper-case letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An upper-case initial is how any sentence of written English is begun.

clue.text: Threatening noises made by angry bears?

parts.note: the word bears shaken up gives a sword's name, and rattling is an agitated stirring of letters, so the phrase read as wordplay makes the clue's angry bears

explanation.surface: Furious bears are growling menacingly.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: rattling the letters of SABRE gives BEARS, and 'angry' stands for that agitation.
explanation.definitionFit: Sabre-rattling is a display of military threat, bluster and menace without action.

clue.text: There can be one of three

definitions.text: There can be one of three

parts.words: There can be one of three
parts.note: the word there uses exactly the letters of the word three rearranged, so one is a jumble of the other

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark that some place could be one of a trio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' looks like an ordinary opening word but is itself the rearrangement of 'three'.
explanation.definitionFit: A word formed by reordering another word's letters is the device described.

clue.text: Cover over Miss Woodhouse's predicament

indicators.note: over signals the word is turned the other way, read back to front

parts.note: a lid is a cover for a pot or box
Emma Woodhouse is the heroine of Jane Austen's novel Emma

explanation.surface: Jane Austen's heroine faces trouble over a cover-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns LID into DIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilemma is an awkward choice between two bad options, a tricky situation.

clue.text: Wire netting used to create a Greek goddess

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are used to make the goddess's name, which sits within them

explanation.surface: A sculptor fashions a Greek deity out of chicken wire.
explanation.walkthrough: The name spans the end of 'Wire' and the start of 'netting'.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene was the Greek goddess of peace, one of the Horae.

clue.text: You could hardly miss it on the farm!

definitions.text: You could hardly miss it on the farm!

parts.words: You could hardly miss it on the farm!
parts.note: a target so big no one could miss it is proverbially said to be as broad as the large door of a farm building

explanation.surface: Something on a farm is very conspicuous.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'couldn't hit a barn door' mocks a poor shot; the clue turns it into something literal on the farm.
explanation.definitionFit: The great entrance of a farm outbuilding is the stock example of an unmissable target.

clue.text: Doubly appropriate name for a cutter, say

definitions.text: Doubly appropriate name for a cutter, say

parts.words: Doubly appropriate name for a cutter, say
parts.note: a censor cuts material, and a cutter is a kind of vessel, so a boat called this would fit twice over

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a fitting name for a person or tool that cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: A cutter is both one who cuts (a censor) and a small sailing boat (a ship), so the word suits it doubly.
explanation.definitionFit: Suppression of books or films by cutting them is what the official practice means.

clue.text: During leave the money goes fast

indicators.note: during means within the period, so the money word is put within the leave word

parts.note: leave of absence: time away from duty
tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: While someone is on holiday their cash runs out quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like 'quickly' but is the noun, a period of going without.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast is going without food, a form of self-denial.

clue.text: Slight speech impediment …

definitions.meaning: a slight is an insult or smear on someone's name

explanation.surface: A mild difficulty in talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' reads as 'minor' qualifying the impediment, but it is a noun meaning an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: an aspersion cast on someone, and slurred, blurred speech.

clue.text: A single chessman (not the King) can make such a stand

parts.note: single means one

indicators.note: not says the king's letter is left out of the chessman

parts.note: the knight is a chess piece
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: One chess piece, apart from the king, can make a defensive stand.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the phrase 'one-night stand', a brief encounter or single performance.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-night stand is a single performance or fling, so the answer qualifies that kind of stand.

clue.text: … and another, making you sound "'stupid" not "unwell"!

definitions.text: … and another, making you sound "'stupid" not "unwell"!

parts.words: … and another, making you sound "'stupid" not "unwell"!
parts.note: a second speech impediment which turns an s into th, so sick (unwell) comes out as thick (stupid)

explanation.surface: A further speech problem makes the speaker sound dim rather than ill.
explanation.walkthrough: It continues from 16 across: another impediment. Saying 'sick' with this defect produces 'thick'.
explanation.definitionFit: This defect is pronouncing s as th, so a sibilant becomes a soft lisping sound.

clue.text: Mix is about right in this kind of cup

indicators.note: about means around, so the mixing phrase goes round the letter for right

parts.note: to stir up is to mix

explanation.surface: Someone stirring a drink thinks the mixture is about right.
explanation.walkthrough: A stirrup cup is a drink offered to riders before they set off, once handed up to those already mounted.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrup cup is a parting drink served to a horseman in the saddle.

clue.text: Inert gas, not explosive without oxygen, is harsh

indicators.note: something explosive blows apart, scattering the letters
without means lacking, so the oxygen letter is dropped from the word not

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A chemistry statement: an inert gas is not explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'explosive' rearranges INERT GAS into ASTRINGE; 'not' less O ('without oxygen') gives NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Astringent criticism is severe and biting, a synonym of harsh.

clue.text: Trade stoppage, therefore must hide a degree of business

indicators.note: to hide something is to hold it within, so the word for therefore encloses the degree

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore
MBA is the Master of Business Administration degree

explanation.surface: A trade ban, so a business must conceal some of its activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must hide' is the containment signal; 'therefore' is the Latin word familiar from 'cogito ergo sum'.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official ban on commerce with a country.

clue.text: Funny business that may leave one feeling abused, not amused

definitions.text: Funny business that may leave one feeling abused, not amused

parts.words: Funny business that may leave one feeling abused, not amused
parts.note: funny business means deceit, and being deceived leaves a person feeling tricked rather than tickled

explanation.surface: Some comedy leaves the audience offended rather than entertained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' is not comic but shady: funny business is deception, which makes victims feel abused.
explanation.definitionFit: Deception and sharp practice are what funny business means.

clue.text: A bottomless lake and river development in South Africa

indicators.note: a development reshapes things, so the letters are rearranged
the bottom of a word is its last letter, which is cut off here

explanation.surface: A dried-up lake and a river feature in a South African project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottomless' cuts LAKE to LAK; with A and R, 'development' rearranges them. The definition is light: a kraal is something found in South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: A kraal is a southern African village or livestock enclosure, a settlement of that region.

clue.text: Sort of prizes the good French sent back

indicators.note: sent back means returned, so the French words are read in reverse

parts.note: in French le is the and bon is good

explanation.surface: The French return a certain kind of award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns LE BON into NOBEL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nobel Prizes are the famous annual awards founded by Alfred Nobel.

clue.text: Article upset Sarah, sadly

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the name reads from the bottom up

parts.note: Sal is a short form of Sarah

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece distressed Sarah, regrettably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns SAL into LAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation of regret, used like unfortunately or sadly.

clue.text: Rabbit down under

parts.note: to rabbit is British slang for chattering on; down under is Australia, where nagging talk has its own slang word

explanation.surface: Bunnies in Australia, or a rabbit in its burrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' is the British verb meaning to talk on and on; 'down under' points to the Australian slang equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Australian slang for talking incessantly at someone, the local version of chattering on.

clue.text: Run in the army? Not wearing this!

indicators.note: in places the run letter within the word for the army

parts.note: a legion is a body of soldiers, a Roman army unit
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: A soldier is told he can't go jogging on duty while shackled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like a jog but is R; the definition works with the surface: you could not run wearing an ankle shackle.
explanation.definitionFit: A shackle fastened round a prisoner's ankle stops any running, which the exclamation implies.

clue.text: East European place much preferred by drivers

parts.note: a Pole is someone from Poland
a position is a place

explanation.surface: A spot in Eastern Europe that motorists favour.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the phrase describing the answer: the grid slot racing drivers most want.
explanation.definitionFit: Racing drivers covet the front grid slot, earned by the fastest qualifying lap.
